question.text: FRAMING bias means that the same information presented differently can lead to different decisions. Which of the following is an example of framing in a financial context?

answer.text: Investor responses change depending on whether outcomes are described as "lives saved" versus "lives lost", or whether a product is labelled "fat-free" versus showing the equivalent fat content

explanation.text: The Logic: Framing bias means the way information is presented changes decisions even when the underlying facts are the same. The workbook gives examples such as the "lives saved versus lives lost" presentation, "fat-free" versus equivalent fat-content labelling, and the way risk tolerance questionnaires and portfolio-performance evaluations are framed to investors. The Trap: Perfect rationality, "no effect", and enhanced market efficiency are the opposite of what framing describes — framing is a documented departure from rational, presentation-invariant choice. Note: The presence of framing means presentation choices in risk questionnaires and performance reports can themselves influence investor responses, independent of the underlying data.
